claim: Mice deficient in both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 (dKO) had severely reduced adipose tissue.
source: Mice deficient in both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 (dKO) had severely reduced adipose tissue and were resistant to high-fat diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from DEXA measurements, micro-CT imaging, and body composition analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mice deficient in both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 (dKO) were resistant to high-fat diet-induced obesity.
source: Mice deficient in both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 (dKO) had severely reduced adipose tissue and were resistant to high-fat diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing body weight gain measurements during HFD feeding presented in Figure 1F.

claim: Wnt signaling was significantly upregulated in dKO mice.
source: Wnt signaling, a negative regulator of adipocyte differentiation, was significantly upregulated in dKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by TOPflash reporter assays and western blot analyses of β-catenin protein levels presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elevated levels of the Wnt/β-catenin target protein Dlk1 inhibited the expression of adipogenesis regulators Pparg and Cebpa.
source: Elevated levels of the Wnt/β-catenin target protein Dlk1 inhibited the expression of adipogenesis regulators Pparg and Cebpa, and fatty acid transporter Cd36.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and western blot data showing inverse relationships between Dlk1 levels and Pparg/Cebpa expression.

claim: Elevated levels of Dlk1 inhibited the expression of fatty acid transporter Cd36.
source: Elevated levels of the Wnt/β-catenin target protein Dlk1 inhibited the expression of adipogenesis regulators Pparg and Cebpa, and fatty acid transporter Cd36.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing reduced Cd36 expression in dKO cells and tissues.

claim: Ifrd1 acted by controlling Wnt signaling and thereby transcriptional regulation of Dlk1.
source: Ifrd1 acted by controlling Wnt signaling and thereby transcriptional regulation of Dlk1.
evidence: This claim is supported by TOPflash assays, ChIP experiments, and western blot analyses showing Ifrd1's effect on Wnt signaling and Dlk1 transcription.

claim: Ifrd2 acts as a general translational inhibitor significantly affecting Dlk1 protein levels.
source: On the other hand, distinctive experimental evidence showed that Ifrd2 acts as a general translational inhibitor significantly affecting Dlk1 protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolic labeling experiments with 35S-methionine and polyribosome profiling data.

claim: At 10 weeks of age, dKO mice displayed 30% and later up to 44.9% lower body weight compared with WT mice.
source: At 10 wk of age, dKO mice displayed 30% and later up to 44.9% lower body weight compared with WT mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal body weight measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The percentage of fat was 37.7 ± 4% in WT mice versus 6 ± 3% of the total body mass in dKO animals.
source: The percentage of fat was in the WT mice 37.7 ± 4% vs. 6 ± 3% of the total body mass in dKO animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by DEXA measurements presented in Figure 1B.

claim: The percentage of lean tissue mass in WT animals was lower than those in dKO animals (60 ± 4.6% vs. 92 ± 3.14%).
source: Furthermore, the percentage of lean tissue mass in WT animals was lower than those in dKO animals (60 ± 4.6% vs. 92 ± 3.14%; Figure 1B, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by DEXA measurements presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Ifrd1 deficiency caused a substantial lack of the abdominal fat tissues (p=0.002 when compared to WT mice).
source: Quantitative analyses of micro-CT measurements showed that Ifrd1 deficiency caused a substantial lack of the abdominal fat tissues (p=0.002 when compared to WT mice, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative micro-CT measurements presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Ifrd2 KO mice were lighter (p=0.007) and leaner (p=0.0001).
source: Whereas Ifrd1 KO mice had less fat mass but were not significantly lighter than their WT littermates (Figure 1E), Ifrd2 KO were lighter (p=0.007) and leaner (p=0.0001) and dKO mice were both significantly lighter (p=0.0001) and had significantly less abdominal fat (p=0.006) than the WT mice (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight and fat mass measurements presented in Figure 1E.

claim: dKO mice were both significantly lighter (p=0.0001) and had significantly less abdominal fat (p=0.006) than the WT mice.
source: Whereas Ifrd1 KO mice had less fat mass but were not significantly lighter than their WT littermates (Figure 1E), Ifrd2 KO were lighter (p=0.007) and leaner (p=0.0001) and dKO mice were both significantly lighter (p=0.0001) and had significantly less abdominal fat (p=0.006) than the WT mice (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight and fat mass measurements presented in Figures 1D and 1E.

claim: Within the first week of HFD feeding WT mice gained more weight than the dKO mice.
source: Already within the first week of HFD feeding WT mice gained more weight than the dKO mice (Figure 1F), although there were no obvious differences in food consumption (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or in levels of lipolytic enzymes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements during HFD feeding presented in Figure 1F.

claim: The weight of WT mice increased additionally for 30% (30.0 ± 2.3%) when compared with the beginning of the HFD feeding period.
source: These differences in body weight gain continued to increase during the second and third weeks, at which time the body weight of WT mice increased additionally for 30% (30.0 ± 2.3%) when compared with the beginning of the HFD feeding period.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements during HFD feeding.

claim: The weight of dKO animals increased only slightly (7.6 ± 1.6%) during HFD feeding.
source: In contrast, the weight of dKO animals increased only slightly (7.6 ± 1.6%) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements during HFD feeding presented in Figure 1F.

claim: Ifrd1 expression reached maximum levels representing 5.7-fold increase compared to proliferating WT MEFs on day 3 of adipocyte differentiation.
source: Ifrd1 expression reached maximum levels representing 5.7-fold increase compared to proliferating WT MEFs on day 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) and Ifrd2 reached on day 5 the maximum of 2.5-fold expression levels of proliferating MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data measuring Ifrd1 expression during adipocyte differentiation presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Ifrd2 reached on day 5 the maximum of 2.5-fold expression levels of proliferating MEFs during adipocyte differentiation.
source: Ifrd1 expression reached maximum levels representing 5.7-fold increase compared to proliferating WT MEFs on day 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) and Ifrd2 reached on day 5 the maximum of 2.5-fold expression levels of proliferating MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data measuring Ifrd2 expression during adipocyte differentiation presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Fat vacuole formation in cells derived from Ifrd2, Ifrd1, and dKO mice represented 23, 48, and 12% of the WT cells, respectively.
source: Quantification of this staining revealed that fat vacuole formation in cells derived from Ifrd2, Ifrd1, and dKO mice represented 23, 48, and 12% of the WT cells, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of oil red O staining presented in Figure 2B.

claim: Stable ectopic expression of Ifrd2 significantly increased adipocyte differentiation in both single and double Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 knockout MEF cell lines.
source: Stable ectopic expression of Ifrd2 significantly increased adipocyte differentiation in both single and double Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 knockout MEF cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by oil red O staining data from rescue experiments presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic expression of Ifrd1 significantly induced the adipocyte differentiation in Ifrd1 single knockout MEFs.
source: Ectopic expression of Ifrd1 significantly induced the adipocyte differentiation in Ifrd1 single knockout MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by oil red O staining data from rescue experiments presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Wnt signaling activity was not regulated in Ifrd2 KO but highly significantly (p<0.0001) upregulated in Ifrd1 KO and also in dKO MEFs when compared to WT MEFs.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, Wnt signaling activity, when compared to the WT MEFs, was not regulated in Ifrd2 KO, but highly significantly (p<0.0001) upregulated in Ifrd1 KO and also in dKO MEFs.
evidence: This claim is supported by TOPflash reporter assay data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: Western blot analyses identified increased β-catenin protein levels in inguinal WAT of Ifrd1 KO and in dKO mice (p<0.0001), but not in Ifrd2 KO mice.
source: Supporting these findings, western blot analyses also identified increased β-catenin protein levels in inguinal WAT of Ifrd1 KO and in dKO mice (p<0.0001), but not in Ifrd2 KO mice (Figure 2D, left top panel), suggesting the involvement of Ifrd1 but not Ifrd2 in the Wnt signaling pathway regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Dlk1 protein was significantly upregulated in inguinal WAT isolated from Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 KO as well as from dKO mice.
source: Dlk1 protein was significantly upregulated in inguinal WAT isolated from Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 KO as well as from dKO mice (Figure 2D, right top panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: A significant (p<0.001) upregulation of Dlk1 mRNA and protein levels in dKO inguinal WAT samples was revealed by qPCR and western blot analyses.
source: A significant (p<0.001) upregulation of Dlk1 mRNA and protein levels in dKO inguinal WAT samples revealed the qPCR and confirmed western blot analyses (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and western blot data presented in Figure 2E.

claim: Upregulation of Dlk1 in dKO mice both on RNA and protein results was confirmed in undifferentiated SVF cells isolated from inguinal fat.
source: Upregulation of Dlk1 in dKO mice both on RNA and protein results was confirmed in undifferentiated SVF cells isolated from inguinal fat (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and western blot data presented in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: Dlk1 mRNA levels were even stronger upregulated following the 8-days differentiation protocol of SVF cells.
source: Dlk1 mRNA levels were even stronger upregulated following the 8-days differentiation protocol of SVF cells (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 2H.

claim: In WT MEFs the expression of Dlk1 was strongly upregulated only during the first day of adipocyte differentiation and then over the next days declined to basal levels.
source: Moreover, whereas in WT MEFs the expression of Dlk1 was strongly upregulated only during the first day of adipocyte differentiation and then over the next days declined to basal levels, in dKO MEFs Dlk1 was upregulated (p<0.001) throughout the entire 8 d of differentiation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data measuring Dlk1 expression during adipocyte differentiation presented in Figure 3A.

claim: In dKO MEFs Dlk1 was upregulated (p<0.001) throughout the entire 8 days of differentiation.
source: Moreover, whereas in WT MEFs the expression of Dlk1 was strongly upregulated only during the first day of adipocyte differentiation and then over the next days declined to basal levels, in dKO MEFs Dlk1 was upregulated (p<0.001) throughout the entire 8 d of differentiation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data measuring Dlk1 expression during adipocyte differentiation presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Ectopic expression of Ifrd1, Ifrd2 and mainly their combination significantly (p<0.001) downregulated Dlk1 mRNA and protein levels.
source: Ectopic expression of Ifrd1, Ifrd2 and mainly their combination significantly (p<0.001) downregulated Dlk1 mRNA and protein levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and western blot data from rescue experiments presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Pparg and Cebpa mRNA levels were strongly induced in undifferentiated WT cells but were barely detectable in dKO SVF cells.
source: While Pparg and Cebpa mRNA levels were strongly induced in undifferentiated WT, these were barely detectable in dKO SVF cells (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Significantly decreased Pparg and Cebpa mRNA levels in Ifrd1, Ifrd2, and dKO inguinal SVF cells following 8-day adipocyte differentiation protocol were identified.
source: Similarly, significantly decreased Pparg and Cebpa mRNA levels in Ifrd1, Ifrd2, and dKO inguinal SVF cells following 8-day adipocyte differentiation protocol were identified (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: ChIP experiments identified increased β-catenin binding to the β-catenin/TCF binding site 2 of the Dlk1 regulatory element in dKO MEFs when compared to WT MEFs.
source: dKO MEFs treated 8 d with the adipocyte differentiation cocktail were increased β-catenin binding to the β-catenin/TCF binding site 2 of the Dlk1 regulatory element found when compared to WT MEFs (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: Binding of H4R3me2s to the Dlk1 regulatory element was significantly reduced (p<0.001) in dKO MEFs.
source: On the other hand, binding of H4R3me2s to the same Dlk1 regulatory element was significantly reduced (p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: No direct binding of Irfd1 or Ifrd2 proteins to two different Dlk1 regulatory elements (Dlk1 region A and β-cat/TCFbs2), neither in WT nor in dKO MEFs, could be identified.
source: No direct binding of Irfd1 or Ifrd2 proteins to two different Dlk1 regulatory elements (Dlk1 region A and β-cat/TCFbs2), neither in WT nor in dKO MEFs, could be identified, suggesting rather an epigenetic regulation than via their direct binding to Dlk1 regulatory elements.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: Dlk1 expression in Ifrd2 KO MEFs was significantly increased (>70-fold) when compared to WT MEFs.
source: These were significantly increased (>70-fold) when compared to WT MEFs (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 3H.

claim: Significantly (p=8.26104 E-07) higher Dlk1 mRNA levels in polyribosome RNA fraction of Ifrd2 KO when compared to WT MEFs were detected.
source: This analysis detected significantly (p<8.26104 E-07) higher Dlk1 mRNA levels in polyribosome RNA fraction of Ifrd2 KO when compared to WT MEFs (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR analysis of polyribosome-bound RNA presented in Figure 3I.

claim: Ifrd2 was recently identified as a novel specific factor capable of translationally inactivating ribosomes.
source: Interestingly, Ifrd2 was recently identified as a novel specific factor capable of translationally inactivating ribosomes (Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2018.

claim: There was a significant increase in the general translational activity of MEFs lacking Ifrd2 alone or both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2, but not in TIS7 single knockout cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, there was a significant increase in the general translational activity of MEFs lacking Ifrd2 alone or both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2, but not in TIS7 single knockout cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolic labeling data with 35S-methionine presented in Figure 4A.

claim: dKO cells secreted Dlk1 protein, but in an identical volume of the cell culture medium from WT MEFs no Dlk1 could be detected.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, dKO cells secreted Dlk1 protein, but in an identical volume of the cell culture medium from WT MEFs no Dlk1 could be detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot analysis of conditioned medium presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Adipocyte differentiation of WT MEFs was strongly inhibited by the dKO MEFs-conditioned medium when compared to the control WT cells.
source: Adipocyte differentiation of WT MEFs was strongly inhibited by the dKO MEFs-conditioned medium when compared to the control WT cells (Figure 4C, quantified in Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by oil red O staining data presented in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Both Dlk1 knockdown constructs stably expressed in dKO MEFs significantly increased (p<0.001) adipocyte differentiation.
source: Both Dlk1 knockdown constructs stably expressed in dKO MEFs significantly increased (p<0.001) adipocyte differentiation as documented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.
evidence: This claim is supported by oil red O staining data from Dlk1 knockdown experiments presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The knockdown of Dlk1 levels was paralleled by a significant (p<0.001) decrease in Hes1 mRNA levels.
source: The knockdown of Dlk1 levels was paralleled by a significant (p<0.001) decrease in Hes1 mRNA levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment with a recombinant Dlk1 protein or stable Dlk1 ectopic expression significantly (p<0.001) inhibited adipocyte differentiation of WT MEFs.
source: In contrast, treatment with a recombinant Dlk1 protein or stable Dlk1 ectopic expression documented by qRT-PCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C) significantly (p<0.001) inhibited adipocyte differentiation of WT MEFs as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.
evidence: This claim is supported by oil red O staining data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Dlk1 treatment was accompanied by a significant (p<0.001) decrease in Cebpa mRNA levels.
source: This was accompanied by a significant (p<0.001) decrease in Cebpa mRNA levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: WT cells treated with dKO MEFs-conditioned medium expressed significantly lower amounts of Pparg mRNA when compared to WT cells incubated with control medium.
source: In parallel, WT cells treated with dKO MEFs-conditioned medium expressed significantly lower amounts of Pparg mRNA when compared to WT cells incubated with control medium (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: Ectopic expression of Ifrd2 and co-expression with Ifrd1 in dKO MEFs rescued almost up to WT levels the adipocyte differentiation potential of these cells.
source: In addition, ectopic expression of Ifrd2 and co-expression with Ifrd1 in dKO MEFs rescued almost up to WT levels the adipocyte differentiation potential of these cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by oil red O staining data from rescue experiments presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic expression of both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 significantly (p<0.001) downregulated Dlk1 mRNA expression in dKO MEFs.
source: Ectopic expression of both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 significantly (p<0.001) downregulated Dlk1 mRNA expression in dKO MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from rescue experiments presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Conditioned medium from dKO MEFs expressing Dlk1 shRNA knockdown constructs significantly (p<0.001) lost the ability to inhibit adipocyte differentiation of WT MEFs.
source: Moreover, conditioned medium from dKO MEFs expressing Dlk1 shRNA knockdown constructs significantly (p<0.001) lost the ability to inhibit adipocyte differentiation of WT MEFs as the medium from dKO MEFs did (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by oil red O staining data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The phosphorylation of p44 and p42 was upregulated 1.8-fold (p<0.001) in the dKO when compared to the WT gonadal WAT samples.
source: The phosphorylation of p44 and p42 was upregulated 1.8-fold (p<0.001) in the dKO when compared to the WT G WAT samples (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 4G.

claim: Both adipocyte differentiation regulators Pparg and Cebpa's mRNA expression levels were in gonadal WAT samples isolated from dKO mice significantly (p<0.01) downregulated when compared to the values of WT control animals.
source: Both adipocyte differentiation regulators Pparg and Cebpa's mRNA expression levels were in gonadal WAT samples isolated from dKO mice significantly (p<0.01) downregulated when compared to the values of WT control animals (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 4H.

claim: Western blot analysis identified a significant (p<0.001) increase in Dlk1 protein levels in BAT samples in knockout mice of all three genotypes.
source: Western blot analysis identified a significant (p<0.001) increase in Dlk1 protein levels in BAT samples in knockout mice of all three genotypes (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 4I.

claim: The phosphorylation of p42 and of p44 was upregulated 3-fold and 4.3-fold, respectively (p<0.01), in the adipocyte-differentiated dKO when compared to the WT MEFs.
source: The phosphorylation of p42 and of p44 was upregulated 3-fold and 4.3-fold, respectively (p<0.01), in the adipocyte-differentiated dKO when compared to the WT MEFs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Sox9 expression was significantly (p<0.001) upregulated in 8-day adipocyte-differentiated dKO when compared to WT MEFs.
source: Sox9 expression was significantly (p<0.001) upregulated in 8-day adipocyte-differentiated dKO when compared to WT MEFs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Pparg and Cebpa mRNA levels were both continuously upregulated during the 8-day differentiation protocol of WT MEFs.
source: Pparg and Cebpa mRNA levels were both continuously upregulated during the 8-day differentiation protocol of WT MEFs (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: No significant increase in Pparg and Cebpa mRNA levels was found in dKO MEFs during adipocyte differentiation.
source: On the contrary, no significant increase in Pparg and Cebpa mRNA levels was found in dKO MEFs (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Only the co-expression of Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 strongly increased the expression of the Pparg in undifferentiated dKO MEFs (p<0.001), almost up to the levels of WT MEFs.
source: A rescue experiment showed that only the co-expression of Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 strongly increased the expression of the Pparg in undifferentiated dKO MEFs (p<0.001), almost up to the levels of WT MEFs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from rescue experiments presented in Figure 5F.

claim: The expression of Cebpa was also strongly upregulated by the co-expression of Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 (p<0.001).
source: The expression of Cebpa was also strongly upregulated by the co-expression of Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 (p<0.001) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data from rescue experiments presented in Figure 5G.

claim: In the feces of dKO mice fed with HFD were identified significantly higher (p<0.05) amounts of free fatty acids than in that of their WT siblings.
source: In the feces of dKO mice fed with HFD were identified significantly higher (p<0.05) amounts of free fatty acids than in that of their WT siblings (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by gas chromatography analysis of fecal lipids presented in Figure 6A.

claim: The energy content of dried feces from dKO mice determined by bomb calorimetry was significantly higher (p<0.001) than that of WT mice.
source: Secondly, the energy content of dried feces from dKO mice determined by bomb calorimetry was significantly higher (p<0.001) than that of WT mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by bomb calorimetry data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: In inguinal WAT from dKO mice were found strongly reduced Cd36 mRNA expression levels (64% of the WT values).
source: In inguinal WAT from dKO mice were found strongly reduced Cd36 mRNA expression levels (64% of the WT values) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: As long as Cd36 mRNA expression substantially increased in WT MEFs, there were almost undetectable transcript levels of Cd36 in dKO cells treated with the adipocyte differentiation cocktail.
source: As long as Cd36 mRNA expression substantially increased in WT MEFs, there were almost undetectable transcript levels of Cd36 in dKO cells treated with the adipocyte differentiation cocktail (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 6D.

claim: As long as Dgat1 expression substantially increased during the differentiation of WT MEFs, there was no difference in Dgat1 mRNA levels in dKO cells treated with the adipocyte differentiation cocktail.
source: As long as Dgat1 expression substantially increased during the differentiation of WT MEFs, there was no difference in Dgat1 mRNA levels in dKO cells treated with the adipocyte differentiation cocktail (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: Adipogenesis is a complex process in which multipotent stem cells are converted into preadipocytes before terminal differentiation into adipocytes.
source: Adipogenesis is a complex process in which multipotent stem cells are converted into preadipocytes before terminal differentiation into adipocytes (Sarantopoulos et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sarantopoulos et al., 2018.

claim: TIS7 protein has been shown to be involved in the mainly transcriptional regulation of differentiation processes in various cell types, for example, neurons, enterocytes, myocytes, and also adipocytes.
source: TPA-induced sequence 7 (TIS7) protein has been shown to be involved in the mainly transcriptional regulation of differentiation processes in various cell types, for example, neurons (Iacopetti et al., 1996), enterocytes (Wang et al., 2005), myocytes (Vadivelu et al., 2004), and also adipocytes (Nakamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Iacopetti et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2005; Vadivelu et al., 2004; Nakamura et al., 2013).

claim: Ifrd1 deficiency leads to a significant upregulation of Wnt/β-catenin transcriptional activity in both primary osteoblasts and in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) derived from Ifrd1 knockout (KO) mice.
source: Ifrd1 deficiency leads to a significant upregulation of Wnt/β-catenin transcriptional activity in both primary osteoblasts and in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) derived from Ifrd1 knockout (KO) mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the authors' previous work.

claim: Ifrd1 was upregulated in both visceral white adipose tissue (vWAT) and subcutaneous white adipose tissue (sWAT) of genetically obese ob/ob mice.
source: It was shown that Ifrd1 is also involved in the control of adipocytes differentiation in mice and was upregulated in both visceral white adipose tissue (vWAT) and subcutaneous white adipose tissue (sWAT) of genetically obese ob/ob mice (Nakamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2013.

claim: Ifrd1 transgenic mice have increased total body adiposity and decreased lean mass compared with wild type (WT) littermates.
source: Ifrd1 transgenic mice have increased total body adiposity and decreased lean mass compared with wild type (WT) littermates (Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2005.

claim: On high-fat diet (HFD), Ifrd1 transgenic mice exhibit a more rapid and proportionately greater gain in body weight with persistently elevated total body adiposity.
source: On high-fat diet (HFD), Ifrd1 transgenic mice exhibit a more rapid and proportionately greater gain in body weight with persistently elevated total body adiposity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Enhanced triglyceride (TG) absorption in the gut of Ifrd1 transgenic mice indicated that Ifrd1 expressed in the gut epithelium has direct effects on fat absorption in enterocytes.
source: Enhanced triglyceride (TG) absorption in the gut of Ifrd1 transgenic mice (Wang et al., 2005) indicated that Ifrd1 expressed in the gut epithelium has direct effects on fat absorption in enterocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2005 and inference from the data.

claim: As a result of impaired intestinal lipid absorption, Ifrd1 KO mice displayed lower body adiposity.
source: As a result of impaired intestinal lipid absorption, Ifrd1 KO mice displayed lower body adiposity (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2010.

claim: Compared with WT littermates, Ifrd1 KO mice do not gain weight when chronically fed an HFD.
source: Compared with WT littermates, Ifrd1 KO mice do not gain weight when chronically fed an HFD and Ifrd1 deletion results in delayed lipid absorption and altered intestinal and hepatic lipid trafficking, with reduced intestinal TG, cholesterol, and free fatty acid mucosal levels in the jejunum (Garcia et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Garcia et al., 2014.

claim: Ifrd1 deletion results in delayed lipid absorption and altered intestinal and hepatic lipid trafficking, with reduced intestinal TG, cholesterol, and free fatty acid mucosal levels in the jejunum.
source: Compared with WT littermates, Ifrd1 KO mice do not gain weight when chronically fed an HFD and Ifrd1 deletion results in delayed lipid absorption and altered intestinal and hepatic lipid trafficking, with reduced intestinal TG, cholesterol, and free fatty acid mucosal levels in the jejunum (Garcia et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Garcia et al., 2014.

claim: Ifrd1 protein functions as a transcriptional co-regulator due to its interaction with protein complexes containing either histone deacetylases (HDAC) or protein methyl transferases, in particular PRMT5.
source: Ifrd1 protein functions as a transcriptional co-regulator (Micheli et al., 2005) due to its interaction with protein complexes containing either histone deacetylases (HDAC) (Park et al., 2017; Vadivelu et al., 2004; Vietor et al., 2002; Wick et al., 2004) or protein methyl transferases, in particular PRMT5 (Lammirato et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Micheli et al., 2005; Park et al., 2017; Vadivelu et al., 2004; Vietor et al., 2002; Wick et al., 2004; Lammirato et al., 2016).

claim: Mouse Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 are homologous, with a remarkable identity at both the cDNA and amino acid levels (58 and 88%, respectively).
source: Mouse Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 are homologous, with a remarkable identity at both the cDNA and amino acid levels (58 and 88%, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence comparison data.

claim: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) analyses of inactive ribosomes identified Ifrd2 as a novel ribosome-binding protein inhibiting translation to regulate gene expression.
source: Recently, cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) analyses of inactive ribosomes identified Ifrd2 as a novel ribosome-binding protein inhibiting translation to regulate gene expression (Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2018.

claim: A significant reduction of whole protein synthesis was previously shown as a major regulatory event during early adipogenic differentiation.
source: Ifrd2 could be involved in adipogenesis since a significant reduction of whole protein synthesis was previously shown as a major regulatory event during early adipogenic differentiation (Marcon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marcon et al., 2017.

claim: Adipogenic transcription factors CCAAT/enhancer binding protein α (Cebpa) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (Pparg) play critical roles in adipogenesis and in the induction of adipocyte markers.
source: Adipogenic transcription factors CCAAT/enhancer binding protein α (Cebpa) and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (Pparg) play critical roles in adipogenesis and in the induction of adipocyte markers (Farmer, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Farmer, 2006.

claim: Pparg is the major downstream target of Delta-like protein 1 (Dlk1).
source: Pparg is the major downstream target of Delta-like protein 1 (Dlk1).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pparg is inactivated by the induction of the MEK/ERK pathway, leading to its phosphorylation and proteolytic degradation.
source: It is inactivated by the induction of the MEK/ERK pathway, leading to its phosphorylation and proteolytic degradation (Wang and Sul, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang and Sul, 2009.

claim: Dlk1, also known as Pref-1 (preadipocyte factor 1), activates the MEK/ERK pathway to inhibit adipocyte differentiation.
source: Dlk1, also known as Pref-1 (preadipocyte factor 1), activates the MEK/ERK pathway to inhibit adipocyte differentiation (Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2007.

claim: Cebpa is highly expressed in mature adipocytes and can bind DNA together with Pparg to a variety of respective target genes.
source: Cebpa is highly expressed in mature adipocytes and can bind DNA together with Pparg to a variety of respective target genes (Lefterova et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lefterova et al., 2008.

claim: Pparg binding to Cebpa gene induces its transcription, thereby creating a positive feedback loop.
source: Besides, Pparg binding to Cebpa gene induces its transcription, thereby creating a positive feedback loop (Lowell, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lowell, 1999.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is one of the extracellular signaling pathways specifically affecting adipogenesis by maintaining preadipocytes in an undifferentiated state through inhibition of Cebpa and Pparg.
source: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is one of the extracellular signaling pathways specifically affecting adipogenesis (Li et al., 2008; Ross et al., 2000; van Tienen et al., 2009) by maintaining preadipocytes in an undifferentiated state through inhibition of Cebpa and Pparg (Tontonoz and Spiegelman, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Li et al., 2008; Ross et al., 2000; van Tienen et al., 2009; Tontonoz and Spiegelman, 2008).

claim: Wnt signaling is a progenitor fate determinator and negatively regulates preadipocyte proliferation through Dlk1.
source: Wnt signaling is a progenitor fate determinator and negatively regulates preadipocyte proliferation through Dlk1 (Mortensen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mortensen et al., 2012.

claim: Mice overexpressing Dlk1 are resistant to HFD-induced obesity.
source: Mice overexpressing Dlk1 are resistant to HFD-induced obesity, whereas Dlk1 KO mice have accelerated adiposity (Moon et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moon et al., 2002.

claim: Dlk1 KO mice have accelerated adiposity.
source: Mice overexpressing Dlk1 are resistant to HFD-induced obesity, whereas Dlk1 KO mice have accelerated adiposity (Moon et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moon et al., 2002.

claim: Dlk1 transgenic mice show reduced expression of genes controlling lipid import (Cd36) and synthesis (Srebp1c, Pparg).
source: Dlk1 transgenic mice show reduced expression of genes controlling lipid import (Cd36) and synthesis (Srebp1c, Pparg) (Barclay et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Barclay et al., 2011.

claim: Dlk1 expression coincides with altered recruitment of PRMT5 and β-catenin to the Dlk1 promoter.
source: Dlk1 expression coincides with altered recruitment of PRMT5 and β-catenin to the Dlk1 promoter (Paul et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Paul et al., 2015.

claim: PRMT5 acts as a co-activator of adipogenic gene expression and differentiation.
source: PRMT5 acts as a co-activator of adipogenic gene expression and differentiation (LeBlanc et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to LeBlanc et al., 2012.

claim: Sox9, a transcription factor expressed in preadipocytes, is downregulated preceding adipocyte differentiation.
source: SRY (sex determining region Y)-box 9 (Sox9), a transcription factor expressed in preadipocytes, is downregulated preceding adipocyte differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Dlk1 prevents downregulation of Sox9 by activating ERK, resulting in inhibition of adipogenesis.
source: Dlk1 prevents downregulation of Sox9 by activating ERK, resulting in inhibition of adipogenesis (Sul, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sul, 2009.

claim: Adipogenic conversion is delayed in MEFs derived from Coprs KO mice.
source: Adipogenic conversion is delayed in MEFs derived from Coprs KO mice and WAT of Coprs KO mice is reduced when compared to control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Paul et al., 2015.

claim: WAT of Coprs KO mice is reduced when compared to control mice.
source: Adipogenic conversion is delayed in MEFs derived from Coprs KO mice and WAT of Coprs KO mice is reduced when compared to control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Paul et al., 2015.

claim: Dlk1 expression is upregulated in Coprs KO cells.
source: Dlk1 expression is upregulated in Coprs KO cells (Paul et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Paul et al., 2015.

claim: dKO pups were viable, and adult male and female mice were fertile.
source: dKO pups were viable, and adult male and female mice were fertile.
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from breeding experiments.

claim: At birth, body weights of dKO and WT mice were similar.
source: At birth, body weights of dKO and WT mice were similar.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements at birth.

claim: During weaning, both the male and female dKO mice failed to gain weight when compared to their WT littermates.
source: Nevertheless, already during weaning, both the male and female dKO mice failed to gain weight when compared to their WT littermates and this persisted in the following weeks when the mice were fed regular diet (RD; chow diet) containing 11% kcal of fat.
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal body weight measurements.

claim: The dKO mice were slightly, but statistically significantly, smaller since there was a difference in body length, including the tail between WT and dKO mice.
source: The dKO mice were slightly, but statistically significantly, smaller since there was a difference in body length, including the tail between WT and dKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by body length measurements presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There were no statistically significant differences between WT and dKO mice in metabolic parameters even if the measured parameters were normalized to the smaller body mass.
source: There were no statistically significant differences between WT and dKO mice even if the measured parameters were normalized to the smaller body mass (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by indirect calorimetry data presented in Table 1.

claim: There were no obvious differences in food consumption between WT and dKO mice during HFD feeding.
source: Already within the first week of HFD feeding WT mice gained more weight than the dKO mice (Figure 1F), although there were no obvious differences in food consumption (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or in levels of lipolytic enzymes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by food intake measurements presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: There were no obvious differences in levels of lipolytic enzymes between WT and dKO mice during HFD feeding.
source: Already within the first week of HFD feeding WT mice gained more weight than the dKO mice (Figure 1F), although there were no obvious differences in food consumption (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or in levels of lipolytic enzymes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme measurements presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Primary MEFs derived from totipotent cells of early mouse mammalian embryos are capable of differentiating into adipocytes.
source: Primary MEFs derived from totipotent cells of early mouse mammalian embryos are capable of differentiating into adipocytes and are versatile models to study adipogenesis as well as mechanisms related to obesity such as genes, transcription factors, and signaling pathways implicated in the adipogenesis process (Ruiz-Ojeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ruiz-Ojeda et al., 2016.

claim: A remarkable reduction of adipocyte differentiation potential in Ifrd2, Ifrd1 KO MEFs, and dKO stromal vascular fraction (SVF) cells isolated from inguinal WAT was observed.
source: Eight days after initiation of adipocyte differentiation, a remarkable reduction of adipocyte differentiation potential in Ifrd2, Ifrd1 KO MEFs, and dKO stromal vascular fraction (SVF) cells isolated from inguinal WAT was observed, as characterized by the formation of lipid droplets stained by oil red O (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by oil red O staining data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Disruption of Wnt signaling in embryonic fibroblasts results in spontaneous adipocyte differentiation.
source: Disruption of Wnt signaling in embryonic fibroblasts results in spontaneous adipocyte differentiation (Bennett et al., 2003), and in contrast, stabilized β-catenin keeps cells in the preadipocyte stage (Ross et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bennett et al., 2003.

claim: Stabilized β-catenin keeps cells in the preadipocyte stage.
source: Disruption of Wnt signaling in embryonic fibroblasts results in spontaneous adipocyte differentiation (Bennett et al., 2003), and in contrast, stabilized β-catenin keeps cells in the preadipocyte stage (Ross et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ross et al., 2000.

claim: A subpopulation of the SVF of adipose tissue is adipogenic and at the same time has a weaker Wnt/β-catenin signal.
source: A subpopulation of the SVF of adipose tissue is adipogenic and at the same time has a weaker Wnt/β-catenin signal (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2015.

claim: In adipogenesis, Dlk1 expression is downregulated through histone methylation by Coprs and PRMT5 proteins that prevent β-catenin binding to the Dlk1 gene.
source: In adipogenesis, Dlk1 expression is downregulated through histone methylation by Coprs and PRMT5 proteins that prevent β-catenin binding to the Dlk1 gene (Paul et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Paul et al., 2015.

claim: Downregulation of the protein synthesis machinery is an essential regulatory event during early adipogenic differentiation.
source: Since protein Ifrd2 was identified as a novel factor translationally inactivating ribosomes (Brown et al., 2018), downregulation of the protein synthesis machinery is an essential regulatory event during early adipogenic differentiation (Marcon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Marcon et al., 2017.

claim: Both Cd36 and Dgat1 play a functional role in the differentiation of murine adipocytes and their deficiency impairs fat pad formation independent of lipid uptake.
source: Among them, decreased Cd36 and Dgat1 levels were a plausible explanation of the dKO mice lean phenotype since it is known that both proteins play a functional role in the differentiation of murine adipocytes and their deficiency impairs fat pad formation independent of lipid uptake (Christiaens et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Christiaens et al., 2012.

claim: Cd36 deficiency is related to pathogenesis of human metabolic diseases, such as hypoglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and disordered fatty acid metabolism.
source: The results presented here implicate that Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 play a up to now unknown role in the regulation of Cd36 and therefore possibly contribute to Cd36-related pathogenesis of human metabolic diseases, such as hypoglycemia (Nagasaka et al., 2011), hypertriglyceridemia (Kashiwagi et al., 2001), and disordered fatty acid metabolism (Glazier et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Nagasaka et al., 2011; Kashiwagi et al., 2001; Glazier et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2001).

claim: Ifrd1 is involved in both chow and HFD conditions in intestinal TG absorption.
source: It was previously shown that Ifrd1 is involved in both chow and HFD conditions in intestinal TG absorption.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 share sequence homology and a functional role in the adipogenesis, but they use two independent regulatory mechanisms.
source: Surprisingly, although Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 share sequence homology and a functional role in the adipogenesis, they use two independent regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript showing different mechanisms of action.

claim: Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 represent novel players in the process of physiological adipocyte differentiation.
source: Since dKO mice render a substantially leaner phenotype on chow diet, even without any challenge by HFD induction, Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 represent novel players in the process of physiological adipocyte differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The whole-body deficiency of both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 genes led to a stronger phenotype when compared to single knockouts of Ifrd1 or Ifrd2.
source: The fact that these two genes use independent mechanisms of action supported by the observation that whole-body deficiency of both genes led to a stronger phenotype when compared to single knockouts of Ifrd1 or Ifrd2.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data from single and double knockout mice presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ifrd1 regulates the Wnt signaling pathway activity and restricts Dlk1 protein levels, thereby allowing adipocyte differentiation.
source: Ifrd1 regulates the Wnt signaling pathway activity and restricts Dlk1 protein levels, thereby allowing adipocyte differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by TOPflash assays, ChIP experiments, and western blot analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells lacking Ifrd2 have significantly upregulated translational activity.
source: In contrast, Ifrd2 KO did not affect Wnt signaling, but as we show here, cells lacking Ifrd2 have significantly upregulated translational activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by metabolic labeling experiments with 35S-methionine presented in the manuscript.

claim: Strongly enriched Dlk1 mRNA concentrations were identified specifically in polyribosomes isolated from Ifrd2 knockout MEFs when compared to the WT MEFs.
source: In addition, strongly enriched Dlk1 mRNA concentrations were identified specifically in polyribosomes isolated from Ifrd2 knockout MEFs when compared to the WT MEFs.
evidence: This claim is supported by polyribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Enriched Dlk1 mRNA in polyribosomes was true also for dKO, but not for the single Ifrd1 knockout cells.
source: This was true also for dKO, but not for the single Ifrd1 knockout cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by polyribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ablation of both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 genes significantly affected the expression of genes essential for adipocyte differentiation and function.
source: The ablation of both Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 genes significantly affected the expression of genes essential for adipocyte differentiation and function.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing altered expression of Pparg, Cebpa, Cd36, and Dgat1 presented in the manuscript.

claim: dKO mice were phenotypically similar to both Cd36-deficient and Dlk1 transgenic mice, namely in decreased amounts of WAT and resistance to HFD-induced obesity.
source: dKO mice were phenotypically similar to both Cd36-deficient and Dlk1 transgenic mice, namely in decreased amounts of WAT and resistance to HFD-induced obesity.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the dKO phenotype with previously published phenotypes of Cd36-deficient and Dlk1 transgenic mice.

claim: Overexpression of Ifrd1 caused increased intestinal lipid transport, resulting in elevated body weight gain during HFD feeding.
source: Previous studies showed that overexpression of Ifrd1 caused increased intestinal lipid transport, resulting in elevated body weight gain during HFD feeding (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Knockout of Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 impaired absorption of free fatty acids from the lumen into enterocytes and reduced rate of fat absorption from intestines into the circulation.
source: Knockout of Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 impaired absorption of free fatty acids from the lumen into enterocytes and reduced rate of fat absorption from intestines into the circulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the higher fecal fat content and energy content in dKO mice.

claim: Higher concentrations of free fatty acids in the feces of dKO mice suggested that mice lacking Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 suffer from an intestinal lipid uptake deficiency.
source: Simultaneously, higher concentrations of free fatty acids in the feces of dKO mice (Figure 6A) suggested that mice lacking Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 suffer from an intestinal lipid uptake deficiency, yet another contributing reason for the lean phenotype of these mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the fecal fat analysis data presented in Figure 6A.

claim: Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 acted after the commitment to the preadipocyte stage.
source: Ifrd1 and Ifrd2 acted after the commitment to the preadipocyte stage since the elevated Dlk1 and β-catenin levels found in WAT of dKO mice were characteristic of the preadipocyte stage (Gautam et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the elevated Dlk1 and β-catenin levels and supported by citation to Gautam et al., 2017.

claim: A subpopulation of the SVF of adipose tissue with weaker Wnt/β-catenin signal is adipogenic.
source: A subpopulation of the SVF of adipose tissue is adipogenic and at the same time has a weaker Wnt/β-catenin signal (Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2015.

claim: Nakamura et al. showed that following the Ifrd1 overexpression in adipocytes Wnt/β-catenin signaling was upregulated and inhibited oil red O staining.
source: It has to be mentioned that the data presented here differ from those published by Nakamura et al., who showed that following the Ifrd1 overexpression in adipocytes Wnt/β-catenin signaling was upregulated and inhibited oil red O staining (Nakamura et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2013.

claim: Ifrd1 was found to be ubiquitously expressed in all WT mouse organs without any pretreatment such as hypoxia.
source: Moreover, Ifrd1 was found to be ubiquitously expressed in all WT mouse organs without any pretreatment such as hypoxia.
evidence: This claim is supported by expression analysis data from the authors' work.

claim: Nakamura et al. identified upregulated Ifrd1 expression levels in WAT of obesity model mice.
source: On the other hand, Nakamura et al. identified upregulated Ifrd1 expression levels in WAT of obesity model mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2013.

claim: Elevated levels of the cleaved ectodomain of Dlk1 have been correlated with reduced expression of Pparg.
source: It was previously shown that elevated levels of the cleaved ectodomain of Dlk1 have been correlated with reduced expression of Pparg (Lee et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2003.

claim: Dlk1 protein carries a protease cleavage site in its extracellular domain.
source: Dlk1 protein carries a protease cleavage site in its extracellular domain (Lee et al., 1995) and is secreted.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 1995.

claim: The extracellular domain of Dlk1 is cleaved by ADAM17, TNF-α converting enzyme to generate the biologically active soluble Dlk1.
source: The extracellular domain of Dlk1 is cleaved by ADAM17, TNF-α converting enzyme to generate the biologically active soluble Dlk1 (Wang and Sul, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang and Sul, 2009.

claim: DLK1 mRNA and protein levels are high in preadipocytes, but Dlk1 expression is absent in mature adipocytes.
source: DLK1 mRNA and protein levels are high in preadipocytes, but Dlk1 expression is absent in mature adipocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Adding soluble Dlk1 to the medium inhibits adipogenesis.
source: Hence, adding soluble Dlk1 to the medium inhibits adipogenesis (Garcés et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Garcés et al., 1999.

claim: Soluble Dlk1 protein activates MEK/ERK signaling, which is required for inhibition of adipogenesis.
source: Previous studies showed that soluble Dlk1 protein activates MEK/ERK signaling, which is required for inhibition of adipogenesis (Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2007.

claim: Activation of MEK/ERK by Dlk1 was shown to upregulate the expression of the transcription factor Sox9, resulting in the inhibition of adipogenesis.
source: Previously, activation of MEK/ERK by Dlk1 was shown to upregulate the expression of the transcription factor Sox9, resulting in the inhibition of adipogenesis (Sul, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sul, 2009.

claim: Hes1 levels, together with Dlk1, are continuously downregulated during the process of adipogenesis while Pparg are rising.
source: It is known from the literature that Hes1 levels, together with Dlk1, are continuously downregulated during the process of adipogenesis while Pparg are rising (Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2010.

claim: Pparg induces the expression of Cd36, a very long chain fatty acids (VLCFA) transporter in heart, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissues.
source: Pparg induces the expression of Cd36, a very long chain fatty acids (VLCFA) transporter in heart, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissues (Coburn et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Coburn et al., 2000.

claim: Cd36 null mice exhibit elevated circulating LCFA and TG levels consistent with the phenotype of dKO mice.
source: Interestingly, Cd36 null mice exhibit elevated circulating LCFA and TG levels consistent with the phenotype of dKO mice and Cd36 deficiency partially protected from HFD-induced insulin resistance (Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2016.

claim: Cd36 deficiency partially protected from HFD-induced insulin resistance.
source: Interestingly, Cd36 null mice exhibit elevated circulating LCFA and TG levels consistent with the phenotype of dKO mice and Cd36 deficiency partially protected from HFD-induced insulin resistance (Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2016.

claim: Dgat1 is a protein associated with the enterocytic TG absorption and intracellular lipid processing.
source: Diacylglycerol acyltransferase 1 (Dgat1), a protein associated with the enterocytic TG absorption and intracellular lipid processing (Nozaki et al., 1999), is besides Cd36 another target gene of adipogenesis master regulator Pparg (Koliwad et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nozaki et al., 1999.

claim: Dgat1 is a target gene of adipogenesis master regulator Pparg.
source: Diacylglycerol acyltransferase 1 (Dgat1), a protein associated with the enterocytic TG absorption and intracellular lipid processing (Nozaki et al., 1999), is besides Cd36 another target gene of adipogenesis master regulator Pparg (Koliwad et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Koliwad et al., 2010.

claim: Dgat1 mRNA levels are strongly upregulated during adipocyte differentiation.
source: Dgat1 mRNA levels are strongly upregulated during adipocyte differentiation (Cases et al., 1998), its promoter region contains a Pparg binding site (Ludwig et al., 2002), and Dgat1 is also negatively regulated by the MEK/ERK pathway (Tsai et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cases et al., 1998.

claim: The Dgat1 promoter region contains a Pparg binding site.
source: Dgat1 mRNA levels are strongly upregulated during adipocyte differentiation (Cases et al., 1998), its promoter region contains a Pparg binding site (Ludwig et al., 2002), and Dgat1 is also negatively regulated by the MEK/ERK pathway (Tsai et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ludwig et al., 2002.

claim: Dgat1 is negatively regulated by the MEK/ERK pathway.
source: Dgat1 mRNA levels are strongly upregulated during adipocyte differentiation (Cases et al., 1998), its promoter region contains a Pparg binding site (Ludwig et al., 2002), and Dgat1 is also negatively regulated by the MEK/ERK pathway (Tsai et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2007.

claim: Dgat1 expression was shown to be increased in Ifrd1 transgenic mice.
source: Dgat1 expression was shown to be increased in Ifrd1 transgenic mice (Wang et al., 2005), and its expression was decreased in the gut of HFD-fed Ifrd1 KO mice (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2005.

claim: Dgat1 expression was decreased in the gut of HFD-fed Ifrd1 KO mice.
source: Dgat1 expression was shown to be increased in Ifrd1 transgenic mice (Wang et al., 2005), and its expression was decreased in the gut of HFD-fed Ifrd1 KO mice (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2010.

claim: Dgat1 expression in adipocytes and inguinal WAT is upregulated by Pparg activation.
source: Importantly, Dgat1 expression in adipocytes and inguinal WAT is upregulated by Pparg activation (Koliwad et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Koliwad et al., 2010.
